raw_payload.title: Page Fault Definition
raw_payload.content_text: A page fault occurs when a process references a virtual page that is not currently present in physical memory. The operating system handles the fault and may load the required page from secondary storage.

raw_payload.title: Page Fault Handling Steps
raw_payload.content_text: When a page fault occurs, the operating system checks whether the memory access is valid, locates the required page, loads it into a free frame or replaces another page, updates the page table, and resumes the interrupted process.

raw_payload.title: Purpose of Virtual Memory
raw_payload.content_text: Virtual memory gives each process a logical address space that can be larger than the available physical memory. It also supports isolation between processes and allows memory pages to be loaded only when needed.

raw_payload.title: Recursion and the Base Case
raw_payload.content_text: A recursive function calls itself to solve a smaller version of a problem. A base case defines the condition that stops further recursive calls. Without a reachable base case, the call stack may continue to grow until a stack overflow occurs.

raw_payload.title: Recursion Compared with Iteration
raw_payload.content_text: Recursion repeats work through function calls, while iteration repeats work through loops. Both approaches can solve repeated subproblems, but recursion uses the call stack and requires a stopping condition.

raw_payload.title: Process Memory Layout
raw_payload.content_text: A process memory image commonly contains code, data, heap, and stack regions. The heap stores dynamically allocated memory, while the stack stores function calls, local variables, and return information.
